sections.title: Taxonomy and general form
sections.text: Pestalotiopsis microspora (Speg.) G.C. Zhao & Nan Li is a filamentous ascomycete in the order Amphisphaeriales. Index Fungorum and NCBI place it in Sporocadaceae; some earlier publications used Pestalotiopsidaceae or Amphisphaeriaceae. It does not form a cap or stalk. Its basionym is Pestalotia microspora Speg. (1880).

sections.title: Conidia and identification
sections.text: Typical asexual conidia are fusiform, often slightly curved, and have four transverse septa dividing them into five cells. The three median cells are brown to olivaceous; the two terminal cells remain hyaline. The apical cell usually bears two to four slender filiform appendages, and the basal cell one shorter appendage. Dimensions and pigmentation vary among isolates. Closely related species share this morphology, so appearance alone, or identification from a single marker, may not securely confirm the species.

sections.title: Colonies and substrates
sections.text: On nutrient media, described isolates form cottony white to grey colonies, sometimes zonate, with small dark acervular conidiomata; colonies may yellow as they age and their appearance depends on the medium. On plants, the fungus has been reported as a symptomless endophyte, a saprophyte on plant debris, and a cause of diseases such as leaf spots or blight, cankers, and rots. Its ecological role and true host range remain uncertain, partly because older reports may include closely related species.

sections.title: Use and caution
sections.text: This is a microscopic plant-associated mould, not a mushroom for food. The entry summarizes documented features and cannot identify an unknown mould without specialist examination.

traits: Filamentous ascomycete mould; no cap-and-stem fruiting body
Fusiform conidia with four septa and five cells; three brown to olivaceous median cells and hyaline end cells
Conidial appendages are usually two to four slender apical filaments and one shorter basal filament
Cultures are often cottony, white to grey, and zonate, with small dark conidiomata; appearance varies with isolate and medium
Reported as a plant endophyte, saprophyte, or opportunistic pathogen; species identification may be uncertain without molecular data
safetyNote: Microscopic mould not intended for consumption. Morphology alone does not guarantee a reliable species identification; do not use this entry to identify or eat an unknown organism.
